quote: The result is a film that looks and feels like a parody, becoming at times so absurd it's almost fun.
The film seems incapable of imagining what its protagonist was like in private moments or ascribing any interior complexity to him.
Colorful, stiff biopic starring an over-the-top Dennis Quaid. [Full review in Spanish]
Ultimately, Reagan is an insubstantive Greatest Hits compendium LP existing to spin, spin, spin positive, no matter what.
Jumping timelines and hitting rom a Russian POV make this eccentric biopic hard to follow. However, it does highlight beautifully crafted performances from Dennis Quaid and Penelope Ann Miller
This by-the-numbers biopic is a soggy, second-rate attempt at myth-making that cares more about legacy than about who the man behind the legend really was.

A piecemeal approach is hardly the way to approach a politician who shifted the direction of his party. There’s a lot to unearth here but “Reagan” doesn’t want to be groundbreaking. It settles for stirring a little soil, not moving a lot of dirt.
Reagan captures a bygone era of dignity, class, and conviction in political leadership that feels refreshing.
Reagan harps on the phrase “clarity is power,” and it is clarity as a visual storytelling value more than patriotism or reason that makes this film into the most effective kind of propaganda.
This is not an exploration, but a celebration, and for that reason it's undramatic.
Fans of Reagan will like it…fans of history, not so much.
Though its years spent in development hell likely preclude the possibility, it has the artificial sheen of generative AI, as if someone fed “reverent biopic of Ronald Reagan” into an algorithm.
It will likely be cherished by those who care less about film than they do about Reagan.

Reagan can’t even trace the broad outlines of your stock biopic, because it refuses to allow in its protagonist any kind of complicating flaw, and the geopolitical stalemate that acts as the primary conflict is too big and abstract for the frame.

On the other hand, those with admiration in their heart for Reagan will be able to look past all the problems. They will only see a story that reminds them of how a Hollywood actor rose to become the most powerful person on the planet.
Those who are looking for a film about Reagan the man will not find much of that here. Instead they get a full view of Reagan the politician.

The new biopic leans into this nostalgia with ahistorical bravado and selective story-telling. If you are looking for a more thought-provoking cinematic dive into a critical part of history, you’ll need to look elsewhere.
Like Reagan the actor and Reagan the president, Reagan the new movie has a strained relationship with reality.
It’s a bio-pic of Ronald Reagan from the director of “Baby Geniuses and the Mystery of the Crown Jewels,” “Cats & Dogs 3: Paws Unite,” and “Bratz.”
As a film, Reagan is about as perfect a biopic as you will get.
Without any lifelike characters, it’s hard to find oneself caring, and thus, Reagan’s dedication to such narrow themes proves limiting.
The result is a political biopic with the heartbeat of a faith-based drama — earnest and aiming to inspire rather than provoke.
The lack of complexity in the characters leaves the story feeling empty.
Lets grandpa relive all his favorite soundbites.
“Reagan” is wake-up call about the evils of communism, which, without study, is almost impossible to spot. This warm, fuzzy biopic attempts to blow the whistle.
It comes so close to parody that it brings to mind the “Saturday Night Live” “Mastermind” skit.

A disingenuous collection of the greatest hits played for the fans that neglects any of the flaws or the consequences of his policies, narrated by the Russians(!) and created by those who support a candidate their Cold War hero likely would have condemned
A children’s film for the adult diaper set.

A shamelessly adoring biopic that is single-handedly rescued from worshipful ignominy by its star, Dennis Quaid, who stubbornly chips through the script’s plaster façade to offer glimpses of a man who spent his entire career concealing his complexities.
Reagan doesn’t go so far as to paint the late president as flawless, but even his mistakes are presented as faith-driven ones.
In the end, Reagan is serviceable but not much beyond that.

It’s a thin line between satire and self-parody, and more sophisticated directors than McNamara have tripped all over it. Reagan looks a bit like a berserk Saturday Night Live sketch, or maybe a biopic parody à la Walk Hard...
A fawning biopic light on subtlety.

It would be too easy to rip apart this film based on its perception of Ronald Reagan and its cringe-conservative propaganda tone. There is no need to do so because the direction and screenplay are inept, regardless of message or intent

The greatest sin of Reagan, though, is not its warped worldview, which is to be expected, but that for a movie about a man who puts himself at the center of a world apparently on the brink of annihilation, Reagan lacks any drama at all.
A hollow portrait...
The movie as a whole isn’t awful, and it’s interesting to see Reagan’s life and anti-communist crusade through the lens of his religious faith.

Director Sean McNamara is tasked with giving the audience a hit parade of Reagan’s musings, accomplishments and ambitions, but always with the hint that a vaguely satirical, even humorous version could lie just beneath the surface.
Made up to look like Reagan, Quaid instead resembles one of those puppets from Genesis’s “Land of Confusion” video; the movie does him no favors by showing footage of that video at one point.

It’s one thing to go the route of hagiography and never mention the notable failures of Reagan and his presidenc...but Reagan makes the stranger choice to give voice to the issues of his conservatism and then, promptly, forget all about them.
“Reagan” fails by emphasizing too much and adding up to too little.

By the numbers, but succeeds in its primary objective: to provide fan service for the aging cohort of Reagan partisans, inviting them to enjoy his catchphrases, much the way they might cheer for Rocky or Iron Man.
The intended audience for Reagan is crystal clear, and those who lean conservative will likely find no fault in the way the 40th President of the United States is portrayed throughout.

Reagan’s character, actions, and political savvy were sometimes disguised as upbeat, wonky optimism.  The larger-than-life, outlandish story of Reagan and the Reds is nothing short of astounding.  And then there’s the Nancy and Ron love story.
The Gipper gets a goober of a biopic -- schmaltzy, hagiographic and ham-handed -- though Dennis Quaid nails the portrait of his self-effacing charm hiding a steely resolve.
Regardless of how you feel about Ronald Reagan the president, most will be united in finding this biopic a preachy, plodding, graceless groaner.

Had Reagan done some serious pruning and strictly depicted the president’s tenure during the Cold War, there might’ve been something here. Those portions of the film are slanted historically, but in dramatic terms they’re the strongest elements here.

A cradle-to-almost-grave look at the 40th President of the United States, Reagan covers a lot of ground and does so respectfully but at a gallop that doesn’t allow for deep exploration or any new information.

Even at a ponderous 135 minutes, director Sean McNamara’s ineptly made effort fails to provide any actual insight into its subject’s life, instead opting for a bluntly one-sided hagiography which depicts Reagan as a near-godlike figure.
It’s less an insightful look at the man and more of a fawning idealization promoting a political viewpoint.
It is gravely disappointing that Reagan is roughly on par with Bedtime for Bonzo.
There probably hasn’t been a presidential biopic this tedious in 80 years, not since Henry King’s Wilson back in 1944.
There is a great deal more hagiography than history in “Reagan,” a worshipful biopic of the 40th U.S. President that often plays like the cinematic equivalent of CliffsNotes.

A remarkable piece of filmmaking that not only brings a popular president to vivid new life, but puts his unlikely story into the broadest possible cosmic context. Dennis Quaid delivers a career-topping performance of stunning breadth--and depth.
This is a 135-minute film that demands a lot more depth. And, so, to co-opt a political phrase from Bill Clinton, whom Quaid also has played: It’s the script, stupid.

Mannered acting, dismal cinematography, clunky attempts to enhance excitement via gimmicks such as slow motion, and a musical score like a fountain of goo all serve as flashbacks to Reagan-era network schlock.
Dennis Quaid leads earnest biopic capturing a leader of consequence.

No life, certainly not one so monumental and complicated as Reagan’s, can be satisfyingly condensed into a single feature film, of course. But this is a Coles Notes level of biography that is convinced it’s The Greatest Story Ever Told.
Most of the major events in Reagan's life are covered, but few of them are recounted in an incisive fashion.
It all makes for a plodding film, more curious than compelling.
Ultimately, the movie work about as well as Oliver Stone’s W., even though there’s nothing about it that feels like mandatory viewing.
The result is a shallow biography and a hollow piece of political drama.
Audiences who remember the title character will enjoy watching Dennis Quaid bring him to the big screen again.
Reagan is a lot like the Republican Party now; inflated self-importance and terminally unserious.
A bloated, clunky and shallow biopic.
As history, it’s worthless.

“Reagan” takes us on a fascinating biographical journey through an extraordinary American life. It's a well-made and well-acted feature that looks at Ronald Reagan through an undoubtedly sympathetic lens yet without ever turning overtly political.

Fifteen years in the making and definitely not worth the wait, this is a one-sided hagiographic portrayal of U.S. President Ronald Reagan (Dennis Quaid), his story told by a retired KGB agent (Jon Voight) because - Reagan was so amazing, I guess?
The film’s treatment of its subject is belligerently hamfisted, disingenuous, and incurious.
